newsitem.title: ITALY: State auditor says budget will get Italy into EMU.
newsitem.headline: State auditor says budget will get Italy into EMU.

text.p: Italy's state auditor Andrea Monorchio said on Tuesday the government's 1997 budget would be enough to get the country into a single European currency from the start, without the need for an interest rate cut or mini-budget.
"There will be no supplementary budget in 1997," he told state radio RAI in an interview.
"The budget is sufficient to get Italy into the single currency. There's no need for interest rates to fall to meet the three percent deficit-gross domestic product (GDP) ratio."

Italy's centre-left government last week unveiled a package of measures designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire off next year's deficit and achieve the three percent ratio required by the Maastricht treaty to qualify for Economic and Monetary Union.
Asked whether the budget, which contains a special one-off "Euro-tax", would be enough to enable Italy to take part right from the planned 1999 start, Monorchio said: "I believe so."
He called the budget "fairly severe", but said he was encouraged by the decision, because of the Euro-tax, to achieve the three percent goal in 1997, earlier than first expected.

"The three percent in 1997, however, is an extraordinary correction. Therefore we will then need to make a correction which the DPEF (the government's three-year rolling financial target plan) forecasts for 1998 and therefore we will continue to maintain three percent," Monorchio said.

He said a fall in interest rates had not been taken into the equation. "The fact that interest (rates) could fluctuate and bring an eventual benefit is welcome, but we haven't taken it into consideration," he said.
